./docs/04-explanation/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem.md:11:At query time, the user’s question plus recent session context (last ~20 turns, unless configured otherwise) are analyzed to build a session intent profile. We derive a vector representation of the session (e.g. by embedding a summary of recent high-signal turns) and extract key terms (feature names, file paths, etc.). This session context is used to augment the query: for example, by expanding or reweighting the query with persistent topics, or by applying filters (if the user has been focusing on a specific project area, the system can restrict results to that domain). The user’s query is then executed against Milvus as a hybrid search that combines dense and sparse retrieval. We use Milvus’s native hybrid query interface to fuse vector similarity and BM25 scores ￼. For DocRAG, we weight semantic similarity higher (e.g. 0.65 dense vs 0.35 BM25) since document language benefits from semantic matching. For CodeRAG, we use a closer balance (~0.55 dense vs 0.45 BM25) because exact token matches (function names, error codes) are often as important as semantic similarity in code retrieval. The hybrid search returns an initial Top-K candidates (e.g. K=64 for docs, 48 for code) that maximize a combined relevance score. This Stage-1 retrieval is recall-oriented: using relatively high K ensures we catch potentially useful context, at the cost of including some weaker hits.

./docs/06-research/investigations/designing-and-stress-testing-agent-systems.md:94:Instead of relying on a single agent to generate a solution and then self-verify its own output—a practice highly prone to confirmation bias—tasks are split symmetrically. One agent acts as the primary generator, proposing the solution, while an independently prompted auditor agent reviews the output.9 To prevent shared algorithmic biases, the auditor agent is frequently executed on an entirely different foundational model from a separate vendor.9 This auditor inspects the output for subtle security flaws, logical consistency, and strict alignment with the initial product requirements document.9 This review and critique loop enforces reliability through intentional redundancy, ensuring that execution does not proceed to the next node until the auditor agent achieves full, verifiable consensus with the generator.4 Furthermore, autonomous language model-based red-teaming agents are continuously deployed within the production environment to perform background alignment audits. These agents deliberately inject adversarial scenarios and edge-case inputs to uncover hidden goals, sycophantic behavior, or latent vulnerabilities in the primary agents before they can be exploited maliciously.39

./docs/06-research/investigations/multi-llm-routing-and-cost-optimization.md:25:This gateway architecture enables zero-downtime provider migrations and allows infrastructure teams to update routing heuristics without requiring application-level code modifications.14 The AI Gateway evaluates incoming payloads, classifies them based on complexity, domain, and historical performance metrics, and forwards the parsed payload to the optimal endpoint.4 In high-throughput environments, gateways leverage local memory or caching layers such as Redis to track rate limits, active connections, and budget consumption in real time, ensuring that routing decisions are executed with sub-100-millisecond latency.11 For Kubernetes-native environments, technologies like Agentgateway utilize the Kubernetes Gateway API to route traffic to multiple LLM providers (e.g., xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI) via path-based HTTPRoute resources, integrating LLM routing seamlessly into existing microservice architectures.20
./docs/06-research/investigations/multi-llm-routing-and-cost-optimization.md:46:Task-shape routing refers to the dynamic allocation of large language models based on the specific architectural demands and structural complexities of the input query.7 Diverse tasks require varying levels of contextual memory, reasoning density, and structural dependency.29 To optimize compute allocation, queries must be classified into strict structural taxonomies before a model is assigned.31 For instance, an open-ended generative task such as creative writing or deep research requires models with deep parametric knowledge and high contextual recall, whereas a transformational task such as formatting unstructured text into a specific syntax requires low reasoning density and can be reliably executed by small language models (SLMs) with a fraction of the parameter count.4

./docs/04-explanation/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem (1).md:11:At query time, the user’s question plus recent session context (last ~20 turns, unless configured otherwise) are analyzed to build a session intent profile. We derive a vector representation of the session (e.g. by embedding a summary of recent high-signal turns) and extract key terms (feature names, file paths, etc.). This session context is used to augment the query: for example, by expanding or reweighting the query with persistent topics, or by applying filters (if the user has been focusing on a specific project area, the system can restrict results to that domain). The user’s query is then executed against Milvus as a hybrid search that combines dense and sparse retrieval. We use Milvus’s native hybrid query interface to fuse vector similarity and BM25 scores ￼. For DocRAG, we weight semantic similarity higher (e.g. 0.65 dense vs 0.35 BM25) since document language benefits from semantic matching. For CodeRAG, we use a closer balance (~0.55 dense vs 0.45 BM25) because exact token matches (function names, error codes) are often as important as semantic similarity in code retrieval. The hybrid search returns an initial Top-K candidates (e.g. K=64 for docs, 48 for code) that maximize a combined relevance score. This Stage-1 retrieval is recall-oriented: using relatively high K ensures we catch potentially useful context, at the cost of including some weaker hits.

./docs/archive/history/sourceFiles/tmp-doc-ingest__RAGsystem.md:23:At query time, the user’s question plus recent session context (last ~20 turns, unless configured otherwise) are analyzed to build a session intent profile. We derive a vector representation of the session (e.g. by embedding a summary of recent high-signal turns) and extract key terms (feature names, file paths, etc.). This session context is used to augment the query: for example, by expanding or reweighting the query with persistent topics, or by applying filters (if the user has been focusing on a specific project area, the system can restrict results to that domain). The user’s query is then executed against Milvus as a hybrid search that combines dense and sparse retrieval. We use Milvus’s native hybrid query interface to fuse vector similarity and BM25 scores ￼. For DocRAG, we weight semantic similarity higher (e.g. 0.65 dense vs 0.35 BM25) since document language benefits from semantic matching. For CodeRAG, we use a closer balance (~0.55 dense vs 0.45 BM25) because exact token matches (function names, error codes) are often as important as semantic similarity in code retrieval. The hybrid search returns an initial Top-K candidates (e.g. K=64 for docs, 48 for code) that maximize a combined relevance score. This Stage-1 retrieval is recall-oriented: using relatively high K ensures we catch potentially useful context, at the cost of including some weaker hits.

./docs/archive/unclassified-top-level/skills/pr-merge-specialist/research-brief.md:63:The recommended default queue scoring model executed by the agent's internal state machine evaluates the WSEMT score upon every queue admission event. The specific implementation logic relies on a normalized baseline score modified by an aging factor to enforce an anti-starvation policy. The scoring formula is expressed as: Score \= (Base\_Priority\_Weight \+ (Queue\_Age\_in\_Minutes \* Aging\_Multiplier)) / Expected\_CI\_Runtime\_in\_Minutes. The inclusion of the Queue\_Age\_in\_Minutes variable guarantees that even a massive, risky pull request will eventually accrue a high enough score to outrank rapid, small PRs as its age approaches the repository's maximum acceptable wait time threshold.36
